title: Triangle Multiplication is All You Need for Biomolecular Structure Representations
one_liner: Pairmixer replaces expensive triangle attention with a simpler method that reasons about protein-atom pairs as fast, letting protein designers work at scale.
lead: Protein structure prediction models like AlphaFold are slow at massive scale. When scientists want to screen millions of drug candidates or design new proteins, the model becomes the bottleneck. Pairmixer removes the expensive part of the calculation—triangle attention—and replaces it with an equally smart but much faster method for understanding which atoms should interact, making large-scale protein engineering finally practical. It works because the reasoning about atom interactions is mostly local and can be done in a single fast step instead of three slow ones.

problem.h2: Expensive reasoning about which atoms touch
paras: Protein structure prediction models reason about pairwise distances: which atoms are close to each other, and how do they constrain each other's position? The standard way to do this—triangle attention—is a three-step dance: look at each pair of atoms, look at their neighbors, combine the information.

A naive attempt: just ask the model directly "which atoms should be nearby?" Works, but misses the spatial relationships. When you have millions of atoms across many proteins, triangle attention becomes a time and memory wall. Training takes weeks. Prediction (when the finished model runs on a new protein) takes minutes. Drug screening, impossible at scale.

callout.html: Pairmixer removes triangle attention and reasons about atom pairs in a single, efficient sweep.

steps.text: The model reads a protein: atoms, their rough positions, and residue names.
For each atom pair, compute a feature vector (a list of numbers) capturing how they interact.
Apply one transformation to all pairs at once, instead of iterating three times like triangle attention.
Each pair's feature vector now includes hints from nearby atoms, learned to preserve 3D geometric logic.
Use the enriched pair features to predict final 3D positions of all atoms.

paras: The paper replaces triangle attention—a three-step pairwise reasoning procedure—with a single-pass method that computes pair features efficiently. The geometric information (how atoms constrain each other in 3D space) is still learned, but extracted differently.

hidden.name: Pairwise geometric importance
paras: Pairwise geometric importance is the degree to which knowing one atom's position constrains another atom's position in 3D space. In AlphaFold, this is computed implicitly through triangle attention: by checking how each pair relates to its neighbors. Pairmixer estimates the same quantity but in a single calculation instead of three.

The paper measures this indirectly by checking whether the final predicted structure matches known structures (the benchmark accuracy). If Pairmixer preserves structure quality while cutting computation, the hidden geometric importance is still being captured.

heat.caption: Darker pairs have stronger geometric constraints. Pairmixer learns to weight them appropriately in one step.

reads.html: The model learns which atom pairs are geometrically critical, and how their positions link together in 3D space.

Pairmixer computes pair embeddings (feature vectors for each atom pair) that implicitly encode higher-order geometric reasoning via a learned linear transformation, achieving the same information flow as triangle attention but in quadratic time (pairs of atoms) instead of cubic time (three-way checks).

mechanism.h2: Why it works: from three sweeps to one
paras: Triangle attention works by three passes: first, attend within atom pairs; second, update based on triangles (three atoms at a time); third, integrate the result. Each pass is expensive when you have tens of thousands of atoms.

Pairmixer compresses this into a single matrix operation: a learned linear transformation (a set of weights) applied to all pairs at once. The trick is that the weights are learned from data to capture the same geometric patterns that triangle attention would discover through three passes. The model learns: which neighboring atoms matter most? How should a pair's feature vector change based on nearby pairs?

This works because geometric logic in proteins is mostly local: atom A constrains atom B, and atom B constrains atom C, so atom A indirectly constrains atom C. A single well-designed linear step can propagate these constraints efficiently. The three-pass pyramid was overkill.

stages.s: Embed each atom pair as a feature vector
Apply learned linear transformation to all pairs together
Enriched pairs now encode geometric neighbors

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose atoms (1,2) have a raw feature vector p = [1.0, 0.5, 2.0].
This single multiplication replaces three cascading attention passes and runs instantly on all atom pairs simultaneously.

math.note: One matrix multiply per pair, applied to all N squared pairs at once, replaces three nested loops—this is why Pairmixer is 4x faster.

charts.note: Slow but accurate. Three-pass design is the bottleneck.

charts.title: Pairmixer
rows: Structure accuracy on held-out test set
charts.note: Nearly identical accuracy because the learned weights capture the same geometric patterns. Four times faster because one matrix multiply per pair replaces three nested attention passes. Training cut by one-third for the same reason. Scales to long sequences and large screening runs.

items.html: If the learned weights W do not capture all the three-way geometric constraints that triangle attention finds, the model might miss subtle atom-atom conflicts. A poorly trained Pairmixer could predict atoms too close together. Fix: use real structures (labeled data) during training so the weights learn the true geometric patterns.

Even though Pairmixer is quadratic in atoms, proteins can be thousands of atoms long, so the number of pairs grows to millions. Memory still becomes a problem. Fix: use sparse attention or chunking—process small sections of the protein at a time and stitch them together.

A single-pass model might fit training structures perfectly but fail on new proteins with unusual geometries. Fix: use strong regularization (gently steer the weights) and diversify the training set with structures from many organisms and conditions.

When Pairmixer is trained on diverse high-quality structures and validated on held-out folds, it generalizes as well as triangle attention because the model learns to capture the same geometric patterns in a single pass, and runs orders of magnitude faster because one matrix multiply beats three cascading attention passes.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small protein (50 atoms) with a known 3D structure from the Protein Data Bank (a public database of real protein structures). Train a tiny Pairmixer model (one pair-transformation layer) on a dataset of 1,000 similar small proteins. Then use the trained model to predict the 3D coordinates of the test protein (one you held out during training) and measure how close the prediction is to the real structure.
demo.metric_eq: RMSD = square root of (mean squared distance between predicted atoms and true atoms in angstroms); lower is better; RMSD < 2 angstroms means accurate prediction
demo.closing: The demo should show that a single-pass Pairmixer predicts the test structure within 2 angstroms of ground truth, proving that the geometric reasoning survived the simplification. It should also measure wall-clock time to confirm that the speedup is real—one pass is faster because there are fewer operations to run.
